UX Case Study

PalUp

Finding your next meal companion — one conversation at a time.

A mobile app that connects people for shared dining experiences in a new city.

Role

UX Researcher & Interaction Designer

Timeline

January – April 2026

Team

Siyu (Zoey) Ai, Karena Ma,
Suiyang Mai, Xinran Wang

Tools

Figma, Affinity Diagramming,
Semi-structured Interviews

The Problem

Moving to a new city means eating alone — a lot. Communal dishes like hotpot and dim sum lose their appeal without company. Existing platforms like Meetup handle large events, but nothing exists for the simple, recurring need: finding one to three people to share a meal with.

"People don't want a dining companion who likes the same food. They want someone they can actually talk to." — Core insight from user research

Research

We conducted 8 semi-structured interviews with Chinese immigrants living in Seattle (1–10 years in the US), recruited from personal networks. Sessions were in-person and via Zoom. Participants ranged in age and gender, each living alone or with limited social networks.

Affinity diagram clustering 6 major themes from interview data

User persona: Angela, 28 — Software Engineer, Seattle

Key Themes

Conversation > Cuisine

Participants consistently prioritized conversational fit over food preferences when evaluating potential dining companions.

Group Size Matters

4 people was cited as ideal: small enough to talk meaningfully, large enough to reduce awkward silences.

Safety Is a Prerequisite

Especially for female participants, trust mechanisms were non-negotiable — not a bonus feature.

The Bad Cycle

Fewer friends → less dining out → harder to meet people. A self-reinforcing loop the app needed to break.

Design Process

Four iterative phases, each building directly on what we learned.

Process timeline: Research → Paper Prototype → Wireframes → Medium-Fi → High-Fi

1

Paper Prototype

We sketched four core task flows: managing a profile, finding and joining an event, creating an event, and chatting with participants. A cross-team heuristic evaluation surfaced 12 issues.

Most severe issues found:

  • No send button visible in the chat interface
  • No way to leave a chatroom
  • Event creation and home browsing shared the same screen — users didn't know which mode they were in
2

Wireframes — Low Fidelity

We moved into Figma and connected all flows into an interactive prototype, applying fixes from the heuristic evaluation.

Major fixes applied:

  • Added a floating "+" button as a dedicated event creation trigger
  • Added error states to the login flow
  • Separated browsing and creating into distinct screens
3

Medium-Fidelity Prototype

User testing with 4–5 participants revealed two persistent issues in the Create Event flow.

Issues found & fixes applied:

  • Newly posted events on the Home screen weren't tappable → all event cards made tappable across every screen
  • The "Vibe" label confused participants → renamed to "Dining Atmosphere" (Quiet Meal / Casual Hangout / Deep Conversation)
4

High-Fidelity Prototype

A second round of user testing and expert critique pushed the design further.

Issue Found Fix Applied
"Budget" vs. total cost ambiguity Renamed to Budget/Person
Group size unclear if creator counted Added hint: incl. yourself
Cancel/Edit only accessible from My Events Added buttons directly on event detail page
Chat input field below keyboard Repositioned above keyboard (standard mobile pattern)
Mute toggle had no visible feedback Replaced with pinned notice at top of chatroom
Report reason locked after selection Made reason editable before submission

Evaluation

We conducted in-person user testing across two rounds — heuristic evaluation and think-aloud sessions — with 4–5 participants each. All participants were new to the prototype.

Four task flows evaluated:

1

Log in and manage profile

2

Find and join a dining event

3

Create a dining event

4

Communicate in a chatroom

Notable findings:

  • Field label clarity was the most recurring friction point — small wording changes (Budget/Person, Dining Atmosphere) had outsized impact on user confidence.
  • Navigation consistency mattered: users expected the same action to be available regardless of which screen they entered from.
  • The chatroom pinned notice was well-received — participants said it reduced the need to scroll up for key event details.
  • Safety-related features (report flow, profile previews) were expected by participants even when not prompted.

Reflection

What worked

Grounding design decisions in a specific, counterintuitive research finding — conversational fit matters more than food preference — gave the team a clear north star. Every field label and feature choice could be evaluated against that principle.

What we'd do differently

Our participant pool skewed toward Chinese international students, limiting generalizability. A more diverse sample would have surfaced different safety concerns, dining norms, and social dynamics. We'd also introduce quantitative usability metrics (SUS, task completion rates) earlier.

What's next

A matching algorithm surfacing compatible companions, verified profiles to address safety concerns, and an empty-state experience for newly created events with no joiners yet.
